text: Giraffes are the mammals that sleep the least: they need barely ten minutes to two hours of rest a day. Their brief dreams last only minutes, and they rarely lie down completely.
description_end:
Giraffes have the same number of vertebrae in the neck as humans: exactly seven.
Blue or black tongue: It measures up to 50 centimeters, and its dark color protects them from sunburn while they eat.

text: Lake Baikal, in Siberia, is the oldest and deepest lake on the planet. Its waters hold about twenty percent of the world's unfrozen surface fresh water.
description_end: Formed about twenty-five million years ago, Baikal preserves an exceptional biodiversity: many of its species exist nowhere else. Among them stands out the nerpa, or Baikal seal, the only seal species whose populations live entirely in fresh water.
hint_1: Lake Baikal, in Siberia: the oldest and deepest, and a huge store of fresh water.

text: Education is the great engine of personal development. It is through education that the daughter of a peasant can become a doctor, that the son of a mineworker can become the head of the mine, that a child of farm workers can become the president of a great nation.
description_end: Nelson Mandela (1918–2013) was a lawyer, an anti-apartheid activist, and president of South Africa from 1994 to 1999. After spending 27 years in prison, he became a worldwide symbol of reconciliation, equality, and the defense of education as a tool of social change.
hint_1: Mandela quote about education as a path to social change.

text: The harder it is to reach a victory, the greater the happiness in winning it. Effort and obstacles give a special value to what has been conquered.
description_end: Edson Arantes do Nascimento, Pelé (1940–2022), was born in Brazil. A forward for Santos and the national team, he won three World Cups (1958, 1962 and 1970) and became football's first great global idol, admired for his talent and joy on the pitch.
hint_1: Pelé quote: the harder the victory, the greater the happiness.

text: While Napoleon's armies advance on Russia, several families discover that their loves, losses and decisions can weigh as much as the great battles.
description_end: Leo Tolstoy was one of the great Russian novelists of the 19th century. In War and Peace he combined fictional characters with historical events linked to the Napoleonic wars. The work also reflects his interest in understanding how much history depends on individuals and how much on collective forces.
hint_1: From Tolstoy's War and Peace: Napoleon's armies advance on Russia.

text: Invaders from Mars seem unstoppable against human weapons. Yet something tiny and unexpected ends up defeating those who seemed invincible.
description_end: H. G. Wells was a British writer central to the development of modern science fiction. He used stories about time travel, scientific experiments and alien invasions to imagine possible futures and criticize his own society. The War of the Worlds appeared at the end of the 19th century.
hint_1: From The War of the Worlds: Martian invaders beaten by something tiny.

text: In 1997, Deep Blue, an IBM computer, defeated world chess champion Garry Kasparov in a six-game match. It was an early milestone for artificial intelligence.
description_end: Deep Blue did not reason like a person: it combined enormous computing power with rules designed by experts to analyze millions of positions per second.
hint_1: Phrase about Deep Blue's victory over Kasparov in 1997.
